---
title: "Predicting observations the model did not see"
---

The corrected [Natural Stories release](https://github.com/languageMIT/naturalstories/tree/4700daad696e942f5aba23c957a7423d0de66612), described by [Futrell et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-020-09503-7), pairs self-paced reading times with lexical and contextual predictors in ten construction-enriched stories. The pinned data are distributed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. This unit begins with its participant-by-word-position responses.

```{r}
#| label: prediction-index-data

natural_all <- readRDS(
  "data/natural-stories/natural-stories-corrected.rds"
)
complete_prediction_row <- with(
  natural_all,
  is.finite(log_rt) & is.finite(word_length) &
    is.finite(log_unigram_frequency) & is.finite(gpt3_surprisal)
)
natural <- natural_all[complete_prediction_row, ]

prediction_inventory <- data.frame(
  object = c(
    "complete response rows",
    "participants",
    "stories",
    "sentences",
    "contextual word positions"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(natural),
    length(unique(natural$participant_id)),
    length(unique(natural$story_id)),
    length(unique(natural$sentence_id)),
    length(unique(paste(
      natural$story_id,
      natural$word_position,
      sep = ":"
    )))
  )
)

prediction_inventory
```

An observed-minus-fitted residual describes a response used to estimate a model. It does not tell us how the complete procedure will predict a response unavailable during fitting. In Natural Stories, unavailable can mean one response row, every response from one participant, or every position in one story. This choice is the **prediction-unit problem (PUP)**.

| predictive target | absent during fitting | still represented |
|:--|:--|:--|
| another response row | that latency | its participant and story |
| a new participant | every latency from that participant | the ten stories |
| an omitted enriched story | every latency from that story | the participant sample |

These targets are not interchangeable. A random row split cannot evaluate an absent participant or story because other rows from that group remain in training. Conversely, leave-one-story-out validation has only the released stories as transfer opportunities; the response-row count does not create that many independent text evaluations.

## Defining and scoring a prediction

[Prediction targets](prediction-targets.qmd) state which responses or groups are new and which predictors remain available. [Training and test data](training-and-test-data.qmd) then enforce that separation, including training-only estimation of predictor transformations. A [predictive loss](predictive-loss.qmd) assigns a numerical cost to each held-out prediction, while the [bias--variance tradeoff](bias-variance-tradeoff.qmd) explains why a procedure can follow one training sample closely and still vary across training samples.

[Cross-validation](cross-validation.qmd) rotates a row-level split. [Grouped cross-validation](grouped-cross-validation.qmd) instead moves complete participants or stories together. These pages use the same Natural Stories population regression so that changing the split changes the predictive claim rather than the fitted predictor set. The teaching fit omits participant and story effects to expose those targets; it does not reproduce the source paper's validation models.

## Comparing models

[Comparing predictive loss](comparing-predictive-loss.qmd) moves to MegaOrientation and evaluates additive and frame-specific ordinal models on verbs absent from fitting. This switch marks a conceptual break: the target becomes lexical transfer, and the response becomes ordered rather than continuous. The comparison thus follows the course's introduction to [cumulative-logit regression](../regression-models/ordinal-regression.qmd). Its population fits omit participant and item heterogeneity, and the comparison remains conditional on the release's acceptability-selected predicate-frame inventory.

The final pages return to the Provo passage summaries used earlier in the course. [Likelihood-ratio tests](likelihood-ratio-tests.qmd) compare nested Gaussian models; [information criteria](information-criteria.qmd) add fit penalties; [leave-one-out cross-validation](leave-one-out-cross-validation.qmd), [PSIS-LOO](psis-loo.qmd), and [WAIC](waic.qmd) use matched observations and pointwise log-likelihood contributions. Each comparison keeps the response rows and candidate model family fixed.

Successful prediction does not by itself identify a processing mechanism. The module thus proceeds in one order: name the prediction unit, separate fitting from scoring, choose and aggregate the loss, rotate the separation, and only then compare models.
